chapters.title: A Triumph of Surgery
chapters.author: James Herriot
chapters.overview: Tricki, a small dog pampered and overfed by his rich mistress Mrs Pumphrey, falls seriously ill. The narrator, a veterinary surgeon, takes him to his surgery for a fortnight, where Tricki gets no medicine, only a strict diet and play with the other dogs, and recovers completely. Mrs Pumphrey, delighted, calls the recovery a triumph of surgery.

sections.title: A Triumph of Surgery
points: The narrator, Mr Herriot, is shocked to see Tricki hugely fat, bloodshot-eyed and listless; Mrs Pumphrey has been giving him extras such as malt, cod-liver oil, Horlicks, cream cakes and chocolates.
He warns her to cut Tricki's food and give him exercise; within days Tricki refuses food, vomits and lies panting, and the narrator has him hospitalised for about a fortnight.

At the surgery Tricki gets no food for two days but plenty of water, then begins to eat with the other dogs, runs and plays with them and becomes lithe and hard-muscled without any medicinal treatment.
Mrs Pumphrey sends eggs, wine and brandy to build up Tricki's strength, which the narrator and his partners enjoy; he is tempted to keep Tricki as a permanent guest.
After a fortnight he returns the recovered dog, and the unused beds, toys and coats; Mrs Pumphrey tearfully calls it 'a triumph of surgery'.

sections.title: Think about it
points: What kind of person the narrator is, and whether he is tactful as well as full of common sense.
Whether Tricki was happy to go home and what will happen now.
Whether the story is a real-life episode, fiction, or a mixture of both.

sections.title: Talk about it
points: Whether foolishly indulgent people like Mrs Pumphrey are merely silly or can cause harm to others.
Whether there are parents like Mrs Pumphrey.
What one would do as a member of her staff, a neighbour, or in the narrator's place.

sections.title: Suggested reading
points: 'Rikki Tikki Tawi' by Rudyard Kipling; Dog Stories by James Herriot; 'A Zoo in My Luggage' by Gerald Durrell; 'A Tiger Comes to Town' by R.K. Narayan.

keyResults.label: Character: Tricki
keyResults.statement: Mrs Pumphrey's small, pampered dog whose only fault is greed; overfed, he falls ill and recovers at the surgery.

keyResults.label: Character: Mrs Pumphrey
keyResults.statement: Tricki's rich, foolishly indulgent mistress who cannot bear to refuse him food.

keyResults.label: Character: Mr Herriot (the narrator)
keyResults.statement: The veterinary surgeon who takes a firm line and cures Tricki with diet and exercise rather than medicine.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: Over-indulgence harms those it is meant to help; the cure is common sense, not surgery, which makes the title ironic.

chapters.title: The Thief's Story
chapters.author: Ruskin Bond
chapters.overview: A fifteen-year-old thief, calling himself Hari Singh, befriends the trusting writer Anil, who feeds him and begins teaching him to read and write. He steals Anil's money but, unable to board the train and realising that education could make him a respected man, returns the money. Anil knows, says nothing, and offers to pay him and teach him sentences.

sections.title: The Thief's Story
points: The narrator, a 15-year-old thief using the name Hari Singh, approaches Anil at a wrestling match and asks to work for him in return for food.
Anil lets him stay, teaches him to cook, to write his name and promises to teach him sentences and numbers; the boy makes about a rupee a day on the shopping.
Anil, a writer who earns by fits and starts, puts 600 rupees under his mattress; the boy steals it at night and runs to catch the Lucknow Express.

He hesitates and misses the train, reflects that Anil's face would show sadness at the loss of trust, and sits in the rain realising that learning to read and write could make him a big, respected man.
He returns and slips the damp notes back; next morning Anil gives him a still-wet fifty-rupee note as pay and says they will start writing sentences — Anil knows but shows nothing.

sections.title: Think about it
points: Hari Singh's reactions to the prospect of education, how they change, and what makes him return to Anil.
Why Anil does not hand the thief to the police and how he differs from other employers.

sections.title: Talk about it
points: Whether people like Anil and Hari Singh exist in real life.
The significance of Anil being a struggling writer.
The circumstances that can turn a fifteen-year-old into a thief.
Where the story is set and what languages the characters would speak.

sections.title: Suggested reading
points: 'He Said It with Arsenic' by Ruskin Bond; 'Vanka' by Anton Chekhov; 'A Scandal in Bohemia' by Arthur Conan Doyle.

keyTerms.meaning: insincere praise
without boasting; in a humble way
making low guttural sounds
attractive
(here) showing no sign of worry or anxiety

keyResults.label: Character: Hari Singh (the narrator)
keyResults.statement: A fifteen-year-old thief who takes a new name every month and is changed by Anil's trust and the promise of education.

keyResults.label: Character: Anil
keyResults.statement: A tall, easy-going young writer of about 25, the most trusting person the thief had met, who forgives him silently.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: Trust and the value of education can reform a person; the thief observes that Anil would grieve for the loss of trust, not money.

chapters.title: The Midnight Visitor
chapters.author: Robert Arthur
chapters.overview: Ausable, a fat secret agent, brings the young writer Fowler to his hotel room, where the rival agent Max waits with a pistol to seize an important report about new missiles. Ausable invents a story about a balcony under the window and claims the knocking at the door is the police. Max jumps out of the window to hide on the balcony and falls, because there is no balcony.

sections.title: The Midnight Visitor
points: Fowler, a young romantic writer, is disappointed that Ausable — fat, with an American accent — does not fit his idea of a secret agent.
In Ausable's sixth-floor room they find Max with a pistol, who has come for a report on new missiles due at twelve-thirty.
Ausable grumbles that someone has again entered through 'that nuisance of a balcony' and describes the balcony in detail; Max says he used a passkey.
A knock comes; Ausable says it is the police he asked to check on him, and Max climbs out of the window to wait on the balcony.
Max screams as he drops; the visitor is only Henry the waiter with drinks, and Ausable reveals there is no balcony.

sections.title: Think about it
points: How secret agents in books and films look compared with Ausable.
How Ausable makes Max believe in the balcony and what makes the story convincing.
When Ausable thought up his plan and whether he planned it in advance or used events as they happened.

sections.title: Talk about it
points: Examples or stories showing presence of mind.
What to do in emergencies such as a kitchen fire, a choking child, a sparking appliance, a road accident, continuous rain or a family member not returning home.

sections.title: Suggested reading
points: 'After Twenty Years' by O. Henry; 'The Stolen Bacillus' by H.G. Wells; 'The Face on the Wall' by E.V. Lucas.

keyResults.label: Character: Ausable
keyResults.statement: A fat secret agent living in Paris with an American accent from Boston, who outwits Max through presence of mind.

keyResults.label: Character: Fowler
keyResults.statement: A young, romantic writer who wanted to meet a spy and is disillusioned, then thrilled.

keyResults.label: Character: Max
keyResults.statement: A slender rival agent with a fox-like face who threatens Ausable with a pistol to get the report.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: Presence of mind — thinking quickly and acting calmly in danger — defeats force.

chapters.title: A Question of Trust
chapters.author: Victor Canning
chapters.overview: Horace Danby, a respectable locksmith, robs one safe a year to buy rare books. While breaking into the safe at Shotover Grange he is caught by a young woman who claims to be the lady of the house and asks him to open the safe for her jewels. He does so without gloves and is later arrested, because she was a thief too; he now thinks bitterly of 'honour among thieves'.

sections.title: A Question of Trust
points: Horace Danby, about fifty, a maker of locks thought good and honest, robs a safe every year to buy rare, expensive books.
He plans to steal fifteen thousand pounds' worth of jewels from Shotover Grange while the servants are at the movies; he calms the dog Sherry and wears gloves.
Flowers in the drawing room set off his hay fever, and a young woman in red appears, who seems amused and says she will call the police.
She agrees to let him go if he opens the safe, saying she has forgotten the numbers and wants her jewels for a party; he takes off his gloves and opens it.

He is arrested for the jewel robbery because of his fingerprints; the real wife, a grey-haired woman of sixty, calls his story nonsense, and Horace, now assistant librarian in prison, is angry at talk of 'honour among thieves'.

sections.title: Think about it
points: When the reader suspected the lady was not who Horace thought.
The subtle ways the lady deceives Horace and why he does not suspect.
Why 'good and respectable — but not completely honest' suits Horace.
Where Horace, a meticulous planner, went wrong.

sections.title: Talk about it
points: Whether Horace was unfairly punished.
Whether intentions justify actions and whether acting less than honestly is ever excusable.

sections.title: Suggested reading
points: 'The Unexpected' by Ella Edkin; 'The Confession' by Anton Chekhov; 'A Case for the Defence' by Graham Greene.

keyTerms.meaning: a disorder affecting the nose and throat, caused by allergy to pollen or dust

keyResults.label: Character: Horace Danby
keyResults.statement: A fifty-year-old unmarried locksmith who steals once a year to buy rare books and is tricked by another thief.

keyResults.label: Character: The young lady
keyResults.statement: A charming, clever young woman in red who pretends to be the lady of the house and makes Horace open the safe for her.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: The story tests the sayings 'set a thief to catch a thief' and 'honour among thieves'; misplaced trust leads to Horace's downfall.

chapters.title: Footprints without Feet
chapters.author: H.G. Wells
chapters.overview: Griffin, a brilliant but lawless scientist, makes his body invisible with rare drugs. After setting fire to his landlord's house he wanders London naked, steals clothes from a store and a theatrical shop, and robs a shopkeeper. At the village of Iping he lodges at an inn, robs a clergyman, frightens Mrs Hall, and when confronted throws off his disguise and escapes the constable.

sections.title: Footprints without Feet
points: Two boys in London follow muddy footprints appearing from nowhere, left by the invisible scientist Griffin.
Griffin had made himself transparent with rare drugs; after setting fire to his landlord's house he became a homeless wanderer without clothes.

He spends a night in a London store, is chased at morning and escapes by removing his clothes; at Drury Lane he takes bandages, dark glasses, false nose and whiskers and attacks and robs a shopkeeper.
At Iping he takes rooms at the inn; money runs out, a clergyman's desk is robbed by an unseen thief, and Mrs Hall's furniture seems to attack her in his room.
Confronted by Mrs Hall, Griffin throws off his disguise to show a headless man; the constable Jaffers tries to arrest him, but Griffin undresses, knocks Jaffers unconscious and escapes.

sections.title: Think about it
points: Comment on 'Griffin was rather a lawless person.'
How to assess Griffin as a scientist.

sections.title: Talk about it
points: Advantages and disadvantages of becoming invisible.
Invisible forces such as magnetism and aspects of matter not visible to the naked eye.
What makes glass or water transparent and whether a man could become invisible.

sections.title: Suggested reading
points: The Invisible Man by H.G. Wells; 'As Far As the Human Eye Can See' by Isaac Asimov; It Happened Tomorrow (ed.) Bal Phondke.

keyResults.label: Character: Griffin
keyResults.statement: A brilliant but lawless scientist who makes himself invisible and misuses his discovery to steal and attack.

keyResults.label: Character: Mrs Hall
keyResults.statement: The landlord's wife at the Iping inn who thinks Griffin an eccentric scientist and later believes her room is haunted.

keyResults.label: Character: Mr Jaffers
keyResults.statement: The village constable who tries to arrest the headless, invisible man and is knocked unconscious.

keyResults.label: Theme
keyResults.statement: A scientific discovery can be misused by a person without regard for the law.

chapters.title: The Making of a Scientist
chapters.author: Robert W. Peterson
chapters.overview: The chapter traces how Richard H. Ebright's childhood interest in collecting butterflies, encouraged by his mother and a book called The Travels of Monarch X, grew into prize-winning science projects on monarch butterflies. His research on the gold spots of the monarch pupa led to discovering an insect hormone and, at Harvard, to a new theory of how cells read DNA. It names a first-rate mind, curiosity and the will to win for the right reasons as the ingredients of a scientist.

sections.title: The Making of a Scientist
points: At twenty-two Ebright and his room-mate published a new theory on how cells work in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Science.
An only child in Reading, Pennsylvania, he collected butterflies, rocks, fossils and coins; his mother bought him equipment and found him learning work after his father died.
The book The Travels of Monarch X led him to tag monarchs for Dr Frederick A. Urquhart and raise thousands of butterflies in his basement.
Losing a county science fair in the seventh grade taught him to do real experiments; later projects studied a viral disease of caterpillars and whether viceroys copy monarchs.

His research on the twelve gold spots on a monarch pupa found a hormone needed for full development, led to prizes and work at army and agriculture laboratories, and gave him the idea for his theory of how the cell reads its DNA.
He graduated from Harvard second in a class of 1,510, was also a debater, canoeist and photographer, and his teacher Mr Weiherer describes him as competitive for the right reasons.

subsections.title: Species and Sub-species of Butterflies Collected in Six Weeks in Reading, Pennsylvania
points: A box listing the butterflies Ebright collected, grouped as wood nymphs and satyrs, monarchs, whites and sulphurs, gossamer-winged, snout and brush-footed butterflies.

subsections.title: Number and Kinds of Butterflies Collected in Six Weeks
points: A graph showing the number collected of each kind of butterfly.

sections.title: Think about it
points: How one becomes a scientist, economist or historian — reading, observing, thinking and experimenting.
Discussing Ebright's work in the light of what students have studied about cells and DNA, and which field they would like to work in.

sections.title: Talk about it
points: Answering children's questions from Discovered Questions by Professor Yash Pal and Dr Rahul Pal: DNA fingerprinting, how honeybees find their honeycombs, why rain falls in drops.
Sharing and trying to answer their own questions about the world.

sections.title: Suggested reading
points: 'Journey by Night' by Norah Burke; Children Who Made It Big by Thangamani; School Days by Tom Brown.

chapters.title: The Necklace
chapters.author: Guy de Maupassant
chapters.overview: Matilda Loisel, a pretty but discontented clerk's wife, borrows a diamond necklace from her rich friend Mme Forestier for a ball at the Minister's residence and loses it. The Loisels buy a replacement for thirty-six thousand francs and spend ten years in hard labour paying the debt. Matilda then learns the original necklace was false and worth no more than five hundred francs.

sections.title: The Necklace
points: Matilda, married to a petty clerk in the Board of Education, suffers from their poverty and dreams of luxuries.
Her husband brings an invitation to the Minister's ball; she weeps for lack of a dress, and he gives her the four hundred francs saved for a gun.
Vexed at having no jewels, she borrows a diamond necklace from Mme Forestier and is the prettiest woman at the ball.
Returning home she finds the necklace gone; after a week's search they buy a similar one for thirty-six thousand francs, borrowing from usurers.
For ten years they live in an attic, Matilda doing heavy housework and her husband copying at night, until the debt is paid and she looks old and hard.
Meeting Mme Forestier in the Champs-Elysees, Matilda tells her the story and learns the lost necklace was false and worth at most five hundred francs.

sections.title: Think about it
points: How the necklace changed the course of the Loisels' life.
The cause of Matilda's ruin and how she could have avoided it.
What would have happened had she confessed the loss.
How the reader would deal with such a situation.

sections.title: Talk about it
points: Whether English is the characters' language and what clues show the language they speak.
Topics: 'Honesty is the best policy' and 'We should be content with what life gives us.'

sections.title: Suggested reading
points: 'The Dowry' by Guy de Maupassant; 'A Cup of Tea' by Katherine Mansfield; 'The Bet' by Anton Chekov.

chapters.title: Bholi
chapters.author: K.A. Abbas
chapters.overview: Sulekha, called Bholi, is a neglected, pock-marked girl who stammers. Sent to the new village school, she is encouraged by a kind teacher and grows confident. When the greedy, lame old grocer Bishamber demands a dowry of five thousand rupees at the wedding, Bholi throws the garland into the fire, refuses to marry him and declares she will serve her parents and teach in her school.

sections.title: Bholi
points: Sulekha, fourth daughter of Numberdar Ramlal, fell off a cot as a baby and was disfigured by small-pox; she stammers and is called Bholi, the simpleton.
When a girls' school opens, the Tehsildar tells Ramlal to send his daughters; his wife sends Bholi because she is unlikely to marry anyway.
Frightened at first, Bholi is treated kindly by the teacher, who helps her say her name and promises that learning will let her speak without stammering.
Years later her parents accept a proposal from Bishamber Nath, a well-to-do grocer who is old, lame and asks no dowry.

At the wedding Bishamber sees her pock-marks and demands five thousand rupees; Ramlal pays, but Bholi flings the garland into the fire and refuses to marry 'such a mean, greedy and contemptible coward', speaking without a stammer.
She tells her father she will serve her parents and teach in her school, and the teacher watches with the satisfaction of an artist completing a masterpiece.

sections.title: Think about it
points: What made Bholi feel school was a better place than home.
The teacher's role in changing her life.
Why Bholi first agreed to an unequal match and later rejected it.
Why she is called Sulekha near the end.
Designing a poster on the Beti Bachao Beti Padhao scheme.

sections.title: Talk about it
points: How to contribute to changing the social attitudes in the story.
Rights, duties and privileges of girls and boys and how society treats them differently.
Which language the characters were speaking.

sections.title: Suggested reading
points: 'The Brass Gong' by Qazi Abdul Sattar; 'Old Man at the Bridge' by Earnest Hemingway; 'Gandhiji the Teacher' by Rajkumari Amrit Kaur.

chapters.title: The Book That Saved the Earth
chapters.author: Claire Boiko
chapters.overview: A historian of the twenty-fifth century tells how a Martian invasion of Earth in 2040 was stopped by a book. The self-important Martian ruler Think-Tank misinterprets the books his space crew find in a library, and takes the nursery rhymes of Mother Goose as evidence of a highly advanced, threatening Earth. Seeing a picture of Humpty Dumpty that looks like him, he panics and orders Mars evacuated.

sections.title: Scene 1
points: The Historian at the Museum of Ancient History explains that the twentieth century was the 'Era of the Book' and that a single book stopped the Martian invasion of 2040.
At Mars Space Control, the vain Think-Tank, with his huge egg-shaped head, demands his full salutation from Apprentice Noodle and consults his mirror.
He orders contact with the space probe so he can invade Earth before lunch.

sections.title: Scene 2
points: Captain Omega, Lieutenant Iota and Sergeant Oop are in the Centerville Public Library, puzzled by the books; Oop thinks they may be hats.
Think-Tank declares the place a refreshment stand and the books sandwiches; Oop is made to eat one.
Noodle politely suggests the books are for communication, then that they are opened and watched; Think-Tank claims each idea as his own.
After taking vitamins the crew read Mother Goose; Think-Tank interprets 'Mistress Mary' and 'Hey diddle diddle' as signs of dangerous advanced skills and halts the invasion.
Seeing Humpty Dumpty, who looks like him, he believes Earthlings plan to capture him, flees and orders Mars evacuated; the Historian says Noodle later replaced him and Earth and Mars became friendly.

sections.title: Think about it
points: How Noodle corrects Think-Tank without offending him, and how the reader would handle his mistakes.
Whether books are being replaced by electronic media.
Why books are called a man's best companion, and a paragraph on a favourite book.

sections.title: Talk about it
points: How Think-Tank misinterprets innocent nursery rhymes as threats, and personal experiences of misinterpretation.
Whether English is the aliens' language.

sections.title: Suggested reading
points: 'Diamond Cuts Diamond' by J.H. Parker; 'The Cindrella Story' by Kenneth Lillington; 'The Fun They Had' by Isaac Asimov.
